newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Blair says Europe must move together.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Blair says Europe must move together.

text.p: British opposition leader Tony Blair would oppose any EU arrangements which would allow an inner core of countries to press ahead while others remained on the sidelines, the Financial Times said on Thursday.
"The important thing is that Europe moves together," the Labour Party chief said in an interview with the newspaper.
While opposing any fragmentation of the European Union, Blair could not, however, promise that this would make him more reluctant to exercise the British veto than Prime Minister John Major.
"If the rest of Europe wanted something that was wrong, we would be prepared to block it," he said.
Labour are opinion poll favourites to win the election that Major must call by next May, a month before the target date for finalising the EU's treaty negotiations.

Stressing that he sought "a new partnership with business", Blair said Britain was "entering a new era of politics" when "debate becomes less about some final ideological confrontation and more about the values underpinning the government".
He also hinted that plans to subject all corporate takeovers to a new public-interest test could be scrapped, the Financial Times said.
Another policy which may be dropped was the merger of the Office of Fair Trading with the Monopolies and Mergers Commission to create a super-competition authority.
Blair expressed deep concerns about negotiations at the EU's intergovernmental conference on the incorporation of a so-called "flexibility" clause into the EU's treaty.
This would allow groups of EU members to form closer links even if other countries did not wish to participate.
"If what you end up with is effectively an inner core...that changes the whole nature of the arrangements within the European Union," he said.
"If that were to happen, Britain's influence in Europe would be hugely reduced," the Labour leader said.

He was not opposed to groups of EU countries integrating at different speeds but he feared flexibility may be code for a small group of countries forming "a sort of high table from which Britain is excluded".
Blair made clear that a Labour government would not take sterling back into the European Exchange Rate Mechanism.
"We have no plans to do that," he said.
